## Understanding the problem

An element is a peak if it is strictly greater than both neighbors (endpoints can never be peaks). We support point assignments and queries asking for the number of peaks in a subarray.

Example 2: `[4,1,4,2,1,5]` — index 2 (value 4 > 1 and > 2) is the only peak. Query [1,0,4] → 0 peaks in [4,1,4] wait, [4,1,4,2,1]: index 2 is a peak → answer 1; query [1,0,2] over [4,1,4] → index 2 is the subarray's last element, hence not a peak → 0.

Crucial reduction: whether index i is a peak depends only on nums[i−1], nums[i], nums[i+1]. So a point update at `idx` changes the peak status of at most three indices: idx−1, idx, idx+1. Maintain a 0/1 'is peak' array with a Fenwick tree (BIT) for prefix sums; each query is a prefix-sum difference.
k: Peak status of index i is a local predicate on (i−1, i, i+1) — updates invalidate at most 3 positions.
Store peak indicators in a Fenwick tree; count of peaks in [l, r] = prefix(r) − prefix(l−1), clamped to valid peak positions [1, n−2].
Recompute the 0/1 status from scratch for the three affected indices rather than trying to diff cleverly.

a.n: Approach 1: Fenwick tree over peak indicators
a.i: Because peaks are local, we can afford to re-evaluate up to three indicators per update in O(1) each, applying ±1 deltas to the BIT. Range peak counts then reduce to prefix sums. This handles 10⁵ mixed operations comfortably.
s: Precompute pk[i] ∈ {0,1} for 1 ≤ i ≤ n−2 and insert into a BIT.
On update (idx, val): set nums[idx] = val, then for p ∈ {idx−1, idx, idx+1} within [1, n−2], recompute the predicate and BIT-add the difference.
On query (l, r): answer = prefix(min(r, n−2)) − prefix(max(l, 1) − 1), or 0 if the clamped range is empty.
a.t: O((n + q) log n) — BIT prefix sums and point updates are logarithmic.
a.sp: O(n) for the BIT and indicator array.

w:
## Wrap-up

The whole problem hinges on noticing peak-hood is a 3-local predicate; after that it's a textbook BIT exercise. A segment tree works identically. Pitfalls: forgetting that subarray endpoints can't be peaks (clamp query bounds to [1, n−2]), and refreshing only the updated index instead of all three neighbors. Follow-up: count valleys too, or handle range-add updates (then a segment tree with per-node recomputation from boundary values is needed).
